retrieval_query: If Your AI Feature Didn’t Materially Boost Revenue, It Doesn’t Count. Try Again.

trace.topic: If Your AI Feature Didn’t Materially Boost Revenue, It Doesn’t Count. Try Again.
trace.goal: Argue for a stricter standard on judging AI feature success.
expected_facts: The answer should argue that AI features need business impact, not just launch buzz.
It should connect product work to revenue, retention, expansion, or meaningful usage.
It should reject vanity metrics as proof of success.
rubric_must_haves: States a clear business standard early.
Explains what counts as impact and what does not.
Connects the point to product prioritization.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should say that shipping an AI feature is not success if it does not move revenue, retention, or a truly material usage metric. Founders need to hold AI work to the same standard as any other product investment: measurable business value. Otherwise the feature is theater, not progress.
trace.prompt:
Write a blog post in the style of Jason Lemkin about: If Your AI Feature Didn’t Materially Boost Revenue, It Doesn’t Count. Try Again.

Style examples from train-owned source text.
Use them for voice only. They are not evidence for claims.
Do not copy long passages verbatim.
[Style 1]
Dear SaaStr: How Can You Ensure a Smooth Transition When A New Team Member Takes Over a Customer Account?
Add value in the first interaction.  This is so rare.
There’s nothing more frustrating than getting a random email, “Hi, Tony is gone from the company. I know nothing about you, but I’m your new rep. Can we schedule a call?”
Find some way to add value.
One great way is to demo upcoming features / an upcoming release.
“Hi, I’m Jason, your next account exec. I’d love to find a way to help even more. Can I show you or anyone on your team the new AI features we’re launching shortly? There’s no additional cost for them and based on what I can see, they may radically increase your efficiency.”
Not perfect. But much better.
A second, albeit riskier, way to add value is to set up a call asking for “honest feedback on how we’re doing.”
This works, too.  Customers often just want to be heard.  The “problem” is you might have to do something about it.
[Style 2]
Dear SaaStr: When Is It Too Soon to Target Enterprise Customers in SaaS?
It too soon to target enterprise clients when you can’t support their needs 90 days
after
you close them.
It’s sort of OK in the enterprise to promise features and functionality that are sort of there … so long as you deliver them fairly promptly after the deal closes.
In fact, it happens all the time. Enterprise customers will even sign contracts agreeing to buy so long as you implement a key feature with X number of days.
But if you don’t have the team, commitment and experience to deliver that functionality at least X days after you close a Big Customer … you aren’t ready.  They’ll churn or at least, never fully deploy.
You don’t have to have the full enterprise package in the early days to close enterprise customers, especially if they have interest in you.  You’ll get some slack as a new, emerging vendor.  Especially if you have a strong deployment team.
But you have to meet your commitments and promises to them fairly soon after the deal closes.
More here:

Finish the last sentence.
A LinkedIn post must be at least 40 words. An X post must be at least 20 words.
You may provide analysis, opinion, transitions, and stylistic commentary, but specific factual claims must come from the evidence.

ALLOWED FACTUAL EVIDENCE

[E1] Deploying AI without clear business metrics is a mistake.
[E2] Companies that captured AI spend are operating at 6x-12x the efficiency of traditional SaaS companies.
[E3] Folks that are pretending they have AI, or have slapped on some very basic functionality into their app, aren’t seeing any revenue boost from it.
[E4] Capturing at least a few basis points of the massive AI spend should be table stakes for companies in a category where AI spending is happening.
[E5] There is a massive point spread between companies that captured AI spend and those that didn’t.

Now write the requested blog post about: If Your AI Feature Didn’t Materially Boost Revenue, It Doesn’t Count. Try Again.

trace.answer:
The Hard Truth About AI Features Nobody Wants To Hear
I’ve been in B2B software since 1999, and right now I’m hearing more founders talk about AI features than ever before. And honestly? Most of these efforts feel like nothing more than noise. So let me ask you directly: Did your AI feature actually move the needle this year? Because if it didn’t — if you haven’t seen real ROI from your AI investments yet — then you’re doing it wrong. And worse, you probably shouldn’t keep trying. At Least Not Like That. Let me share two stories that illustrate exactly why this matters. Story #1: The Founder Who Got It Right
Recently, I met with a founder who had deployed ChatGPT-style interfaces across his entire product suite. He wasn’t using generic APIs—he was building true conversational agents powered by Claude and GPT-4. But here’s what made him different: he tracked every single conversation his AI handled. Every interaction. Every resolution. Every follow-up action taken. What did he learn? Conversations were driving measurable value. Real users were finding answers faster through chat interactions than through traditional search. His team could triage issues more effectively because conversations provided context beyond ticket descriptions alone. The impact showed up in metrics:
Reduced support tickets due to self-resolution
Higher quality of incoming requests (users prepared for support)
Improved knowledge base adoption (people found information naturally rather than searching manually)
Enhanced UX scores (faster problem resolution = happier customers)
But here’s the kicker—this wasn’t just vanity metrics.

retrieval_hits.text:
2. Measuring AI by “Cool Factor” Instead of ROI
Chris noted customers initially bought AI tools “just because it’s AI” but that’s changing. The mistake: deploying AI without clear business metrics. Snowflake learned early to ask: “Is it generating more money or saving more money?” If you can’t measure 418 hours saved per week or 90% time reduction on specific tasks or real-time ad spend optimization ROI, you’re implementing technology without business justification. The bill comes due eventually.

The Brutal Truth: AI Features Alone Don’t Count
Let me be very direct here: you need to tap into the AI budget, not just make your existing product better with AI features. The real AI budget is going to three categories:
Replace humans
(AI Contact Center, AI SDR)
Augment humans dramatically
(Cursor, Harvey, Claude + ChatGPT)
Highly productive tools that make possible what was impossible before
(Replit, Gamma, AI video tools)
Most classic SaaS leaders are not going this far with their AI offerings. They’re just making their products… better. Great. But that’s table stakes now. And it’s extremely hard to monetize because customers expect AI features as part of the base product. If your AI strategy is “we added a copilot,” you’re not accessing the AI budget. You’re fighting for scraps from the traditional software budget, which is flat-to-down after price increases. Leaner Teams Are Very Real (Yes, That Means Fewer Humans)
The efficiency gains from AI are showing up in real numbers:
Looking at ARR ($M) / FTE across companies:
Cursor
: 6.1x
Lovable
: 3.4x
OpenAI
: 1.5x
Anthropic
: 1.2x
Atlassian
: 0.46x
Datadog
: 0.51x
ServiceNow
: 0.49x
Gitlab
: 0.54x
The newer, AI-native companies are operating at 6x-12x the efficiency of traditional SaaS companies. And this advantage compounds over time. According to Iconiq Capital, AI-native companies show superior burn efficiency driven by faster compounding of ARR.

One thing seems clear to me in AI for SaaS:

Folks that are sort of pretending they have AI, or have slapped on some very basic functionality into their app …

Aren’t seeing any revenue boost from it

By now, you should have:
Shipped AI features that customers actually want
Seen some revenue acceleration from AI adoption
Captured at least a few basis points of the massive AI spend
I’m not expecting you went from 30% growth to 300% growth. That’s unrealistic for most companies. But going from 15% to 25% growth? From 10% to 20%? That should be table stakes
if you’re remotely positioned in a category where AI spending is happening. As I said on our 20VC pod this week:
“Going into next year, you sure better have seen re-acceleration because of AI because there’s so much money there. If you got none of it guys, you had 18 months to not launch a single feature, tap into a single trend to reaccelerate. If you’re not growing faster at the end of 2025 than the start as a founder, I give you an F minus. There’s so much money and you don’t have to be Harvey to get a little piece of it. Twilio and MongoDB and Cloudflare and tons of folks have a little piece of it. A little piece of that massive pie.”
The Point Spread Between Winners and Losers
Rory O’Driscoll nailed this on our show: There’s a
massive point spread
between companies that captured AI spend and those that didn’t.

Replace humans
(AI Contact Center, AI SDR)
Augment humans dramatically
(Cursor, Harvey, Claude + ChatGPT)
Highly productive tools that make possible what was impossible before
(Replit, Gamma, AI video tools)
Most classic SaaS leaders are not going this far with their AI offerings. They’re just making their products… better. Great. But that’s table stakes now. And it’s extremely hard to monetize because customers expect AI features as part of the base product. If your AI strategy is “we added a copilot,” you’re not accessing the AI budget. You’re fighting for scraps from the traditional software budget, which is flat-to-down after price increases. Leaner Teams Are Very Real (Yes, That Means Fewer Humans)
